source.title: Same Concept, Different Directions: Cross-Modal Feature Heterogeneity in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Chung-Pa Lee; Jihoon Kwon; Kyle Min; Jy-yong Sohn

record.tranche_reason: The study examines cross-modal feature directions in sparse autoencoders on vision-language model embeddings. It does not measure neuron-level jobs, the audit shares, or any other version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The reported measurements concern SAE decoder features and latent coordinates in paired image-text embeddings, not neuron poles or explanations of neurons. The paper also reports retrieval, reconstruction, and steering results for its proposed method; those do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study analyses SAE decoder features in CLIP-like joint embedding spaces (cross-modal feature heterogeneity, modality split) and proposes a modality-specific SAE method. It never audits model neurons, scores neuron explanations, revisits InceptionV1 polysemantic neurons or builds neuron-based attribution graphs. It neither tests nor uses the neuron-cleanliness claim. The only overlap is that it assumes embeddings are polysemantic and that SAEs recover monosemantic features, which is background, not a result on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that the same concept can have different feature directions across image and text modalities, and that this drives modality split in SAEs. They show that auxiliary alignment losses trade reconstruction for alignment. Modality-specific SAEs with post-hoc Hungarian alignment keep reconstruction and improve retrieval and steering.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes SAE decoder features and latent alignment in paired vision-language embeddings; it does not conduct a neuron explanation audit or test held-out neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the cross-modal retrieval advantage varies with Top-K sparsity level; K = 32 is described as the best operating point among K ∈ {16, 32, 64}.

fits_no_version.finding: In base and large CLIP, MetaCLIP, OpenCLIP and SigLIP2 embeddings, highly coactivating image and text SAE latents have decoder directions whose cosine distances do not concentrate near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantically corresponding SAE features in VLM joint embeddings need not share a direction across modalities.

fits_no_version.finding: CLIP ViT-B/32 example pairs (baseball, policeman) coactivate at 0.67 and 0.63 yet sit 0.42 and 0.50 apart in cosine distance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High cross-modal coactivation can coexist with directional mismatch of SAE features.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea (2026)
record.problems: The authors note reliance on the linear representation hypothesis and simplified generative assumptions, possible error in inferring feature correspondence from coactivation statistics in noisy or weakly aligned settings, and experiments focused on CLIP-like contrastive VLMs. The feature-correspondence measure is a proxy, not a direct semantic label.
record.rows_left_out: No results on reconstruction, feature recovery, alignment losses, retrieval, classification, steering, or monosemanticity scores were included: they evaluate SAE methods or downstream tasks and do not measure the neuron-level claim versions.

untested.parts: Neuron-pole shares in other LMs, dense or MoE, at any scale.
Reinterpretation of InceptionV1 cat-and-car and other classic polysemantic neurons.
Interpretable-neuron share as a function of architecture, regularization or tools.
Neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models.
Whether activating-example explanations predict held-out neuron firing.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The paper only mentions polysemantic embeddings and SAE monosemanticity as background; it says nothing about neuron cleanliness. Its monosemanticity scores (Figure 8) concern SAE latents, not model neurons, so they are rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and all stated neuron-pole shares.
Shares of interpretable neuron poles across language models, architectures, or parameter scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons and the proposed pose or recursive-generalization interpretation.
Neuron interpretability shares attributed to architecture, regularization, or tools, including the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and comparisons to replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict held-out neuron activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine-distance distributions between estimated image and text SAE decoder features, grouped by coactivation correlation.
rows.measure: Distribution of cosine distances between paired image-text feature directions
rows.baseline: Perfect cross-modal feature alignment would give cosine distance near zero.
rows.value: Feature-pair distances do not concentrate near zero; across the models, the distribution remains centered at a positive value.
rows.note: The text describes the trend across the four models as an aggregate; the figure presents the model-specific distributions. This measures SAE features, not neuron jobs.
rows.check: SAE feature-direction distances in VLM embeddings; no neuron-level measure, so no state against any version. The row's 'observed' refers to the paper's own heterogeneity effect, not a claim version.
